entities.name: Bhagavad Gita
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
A 700-verse philosophical and spiritual dialogue between the warrior-prince Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna (an avatar of the god Vishnu), set on the battlefield of Kurukshetra at the opening of the great war in the Mahabharata (Book 6, Chapters 25–42). Facing the moral crisis of killing his own kinsmen in battle, Arjuna is paralyzed — and Krishna responds with a comprehensive teaching on duty (dharma), action (karma yoga), knowledge (jnana yoga), devotion (bhakti yoga), the nature of the self (Atman), and the supreme reality (Brahman).

The Gita's central teaching — to act according to one's duty without attachment to results (nishkama karma) — has resonated with readers for over two millennia. Gandhi called it his "spiritual dictionary." Oppenheimer quoted it after the first nuclear test ("Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds"). It is the most translated and most widely read text in the Hindu tradition, with a global influence extending to Thoreau, Emerson, Huxley, and T.S. Eliot.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Bhagavad Gita's teachings on duty and detachment have influenced Eastern spirituality and philosophy for centuries, with Gandhi citing it as his 'spiritual dictionary.' Its ideas continue to shape Hinduism and inspire spiritual seekers worldwide.
